bands.why: The easiest fields (3 sheep, par 3-4) are a calm start: a reasonable player pens the flock in most of them (0.79 measured); the losses are mostly tilting back and forth until the 40-tilt budget runs out, which undo prevents for a person.
The hardest fields (6 sheep, 2 wolves, par 6-8) still leave a calm puzzle winnable (0.68 measured); the second wolf adds the losses.
Naive bots should lose: random swipes pen the whole flock in few easy fields (0.18 measured) and mostly push a sheep into the wolf.
A second-row field takes a handful of tilts (median 5 measured), never one.
A hardest-row field takes clearly more tilts (median 9 measured): more sheep to pen, more to plan.

notes: Flock Tilt, four tuning rows on the 0..100 scale sampled at their lower bounds (0/25/50/75), 100 seeds. The first run (2 sheep in the easiest row) showed the twist almost never: two sheep met only 0.15 times per easy run. So the rows start at 3 sheep and every field create keeps must have a shortest line where a sheep stops against another sheep (the twist from the first field). Measured now: greedy wins 0.79/0.76/0.71/0.68 and needs a median of 4/5/7/9 tilts; random wins 0.18/0.19/0.06/0.05; lookahead wins 0.93 of the second row. The difficulty curve is the tilts a field takes (it rises by at least 1 per row), because a calm puzzle stays winnable while it asks for longer plans; the win rate falls only gently. Kill test: the greedy bot pens its first sheep within 3 tilts in 94 % of easiest runs and sees 1.87 sheep-against-sheep stops per run. Most greedy losses are tilting back and forth until the 40-tilt budget ends (undo saves a person from that); the rest are a sheep pushed into the wolf.
